existence.statement: With all coefficients free, existence and uniqueness are not classified for general nonconstant samples. Held bounds and sizes must permit every observation. Constant samples attain likelihood one at $n=\max_i x_i$ and $p=1$. Free bounds can be tightened to the sample extremes, but their real values are not unique. With size held and nonsingleton retained support, a unique interior probability MLE exists exactly when the sample mean lies strictly between the retained edges. Edge-only samples attain $p=0$ or $p=1$ only when the window contains zero or $n$, respectively. Otherwise they have an unattained point-mass supremum. Singleton support leaves an interior probability unidentified. With an interior probability held and size free, a finite integer maximum exists unless constant data equal the finite upper truncation edge and no feasible size can make the retained support singleton. Integer maxima need not be unique. With both size and probability held, free bounds tighten to the sample extremes whenever the observations and conditioning event have positive probability. A held $p=0$ permits only zeros and leaves a free size unidentified among feasible sizes. A held $p=1$ permits only constant data and fixes a free size to that count. Holding every coefficient leaves only likelihood evaluation.
existence.reason: Tightening a window removes only unobserved mass. For fixed size the log likelihood is strictly concave in $\log(p/(1-p))$ on nonsingleton support, with curvature minus the sample size times the conditional variance. With an interior probability held, increasing size concentrates a finitely upper-truncated law at its upper edge. If an observation lies below that edge the likelihood tends to zero. Without an upper bound, the probability of any fixed finite sample tends to zero. These tail arguments ensure attainment outside the stated escape. With both size and probability free, the truncated-Poisson limit competes with finite profiles. Finite winners require a global retained-support certificate. Unresolved face comparisons do not prove global uniqueness or a general existence criterion.

A nonconstant sample identifies the rate on the smallest retained integer window, but the real truncation bounds are not unique. A constant sample permits singleton support and does not identify the rate. With data-compatible bounds held, tighten each free bound to the corresponding sample extreme. On a nonsingleton window a unique positive finite rate exists exactly when the sample mean lies strictly between its edges. All-zero data attain rate zero if zero is retained. Other edge-only samples have an unattained point-mass supremum. With the rate held, tightening free bounds maximizes the likelihood whenever the conditioning event and observations have positive probability. Holding all coefficients leaves only likelihood evaluation.
existence.reason: Removing unobserved retained counts decreases the conditioning probability and increases the likelihood. Bounds giving the same integer window are equivalent. The conditional mean increases from the lower edge to the upper edge (or infinity), giving the stated root criterion. Singleton support has likelihood one for every positive rate. Rate zero is an attained member only when the window contains zero. The uniqueness claim concerns the rate on nonsingleton support, not the complete coefficient vector.

existence.statement: With both coefficients free, a finite MLE exists for every nonempty positive integer sample. If any observation exceeds one, the endpoint $\hat N=\max_i x_i$ and the shape estimate are unique. All-ones data give $\hat N=1$ with every finite $s\ge0$ maximizing the likelihood. With $N>1$ held, the shape MLE is finite and unique unless all observations are one, when only an unattained point-mass supremum exists. With $N=1$ held the shape is unidentified. With shape held, the unique endpoint MLE is the sample maximum. Holding both coefficients leaves only likelihood evaluation on the retained support.
existence.reason: At every finite shape, the normalizing sum strictly increases with $N$, so the smallest data-compatible endpoint maximizes the likelihood. For $N>1$, the shape score per observation is $E_{N,s}[\log X]-\overline{\log x}$, with derivative $-\operatorname{Var}_{N,s}(\log X)<0$. Its model mean tends to zero at infinity. The maximum is $s=0$ if $\overline{\log x}\ge\log(N!)/N$, and otherwise is the unique positive root, unless the empirical log mean is zero.

existence.statement: With all coefficients free, all-zero data attain a nonunique maximum. For positive data, finite-size attainment must be distinguished from a supremum on the infinite-size zero-inflated Poisson boundary. Retained-support certificates settle strict finite winners within their work budgets. Signed positive-count certificates also settle admissible free-inflation ZIP faces; remaining comparisons stop explicitly. With size held at an integer at least the largest count, a maximum always exists for compatible data, but it need not be unique. With $0<p<1$ held, a finite integer maximum exists. Holding only inflation retains the infinite-size comparison with that same inflation. Held $p=0$ or $\pi=1$ permits only zeros. Held $p=1$ requires every positive count to equal the size. Size zero permits only zeros and leaves both probabilities unidentified. Holding all coefficients leaves likelihood evaluation.
existence.reason: At a fixed size the probabilities range over a compact square and the likelihood is continuous, so a maximum is attained. For size one the law depends only on $(1-\pi)p$, giving nonunique pairs when both probabilities are free. With $0<p<1$ held and positive data, every observed positive-count probability tends to zero as size increases, so the integer tail cannot prevent attainment. With both probabilities held and all counts zero, the smallest compatible size attains the maximum. When size and probability are free, a finite-mean path to infinite size has the zero-inflated Poisson boundary. A retained-support bound and complete integer-prefix coverage certify returned finite winners; they do not establish a general face-win criterion or uniqueness.

existence.statement: With all coefficients free, all-zero data attain a nonunique point-mass maximum. For samples containing positive counts, existence depends on comparison with the infinite-size zero-inflated Poisson boundary; no general uniqueness claim is made. A finite nonnegative size held fixed, or a probability held strictly below one, removes that escape and gives an attained maximum for compatible data. Holding only inflation below one retains the escape, with the same inflation held on the limiting boundary. Further holds retain these conclusions. Held size zero, probability one or inflation one permits only zeros. Holding all coefficients leaves likelihood evaluation.
existence.reason: For positive data, profile probability and any free inflation at each size $r>0$, obtaining $Q(r)$. Its infinite-size boundary is the corresponding maximized zero-inflated Poisson log likelihood $Q_\infty$. A finite maximum exists if some finite $r$ has $Q(r)\ge Q_\infty$; otherwise the supremum is attained only on that boundary. The certificate either resolves the required global comparison or stops without an estimate. Holding finite positive size makes the probability endpoints either attained zero laws or zero-likelihood limits. At held $0<p<1$, the likelihood of positive counts vanishes as $r\to\infty$ and the zero-size endpoint is attained. These boundary arguments establish attainment for those held subsets. For positive data, size held with inflation free, and probability held with inflation free, each give a unique maximizer. Holding interior inflation can instead give competing maxima; uniqueness is false in general even with size also held.

existence.statement: With both coefficients free, every nonempty count sample has a finite maximum. If a count is positive, the maximizing pair is unique. All-zero data are maximized by $\pi=1$ with any $\lambda>0$. With $\lambda>0$ held, free inflation has a unique maximum. With $\pi<1$ held, a finite rate maximum exists whenever a count is positive, but two global maxima can tie. For all-zero data and held $\pi<1$, the supremum requires $\lambda\downarrow0$ and is not attained in the declared domain. Held $\pi=1$ permits only zeros and leaves a free rate unidentified. Holding both coefficients leaves likelihood evaluation, subject to compatibility.
existence.reason: Write $z$ for the empirical zero fraction. At a held rate, the inflation maximum is $\max\{0,(z-e^{-\lambda})/(1-e^{-\lambda})\}$, with value one for all-zero data. In the positive-inflation branch, the rate solves $\lambda/(1-e^{-\lambda})=\bar x/(1-z)$, whose left side is strictly increasing. If this branch is infeasible, the unique maximum is the Poisson member $\pi=0,\lambda=\bar x$. For held $\pi<1$ and a positive count, the likelihood tends to zero at both ends of the rate domain, so a finite maximum exists. Its score has at most three roots; two separated maxima can tie.

reference.method: damped Newton at 50 digits on the README log density, from the fitted values

existence.statement: With all coefficients free, the zero probability is the empirical zero fraction and the remaining problem is zero-truncated binomial fitting on the positive observations. A general finite-MLE criterion and uniqueness result for that free-size problem are not established here. All-zero samples attain $p_0=1$ and leave the base coefficients unidentified. Positive counts all equal to one attain a maximum with nonunique base coefficients. Holding $p_0$ leaves the positive-count problem unchanged when compatible. With $n>1$ held and at least one positive count, the free probability has a unique MLE. At $n=1$, it is unidentified. With interior $p$ held and positive counts present, a finite integer maximum exists. Held $p=0$ permits only ones among positives and leaves size unidentified. Held $p=1$ requires all positive counts to equal $n$. With no positives, all compatible base coefficients remain unidentified. All-held fits only evaluate likelihood.
existence.reason: The likelihood factors into a Bernoulli zero-indicator likelihood and a zero-truncated binomial likelihood. The first has the unique empirical-fraction maximizer when free. At fixed $n>1$, the positive-count likelihood is strictly concave in logit probability. With interior probability held, its observed masses vanish as size grows, ensuring finite integer attainment. Factorization transfers the finite-winner certificate but supplies no general uniqueness theorem or winning-face criterion for free size and probability.

existence.statement: With both coefficients free, every nonempty count sample has an attained maximum. If positives occur it is unique, with $\hat p=1/\bar x_+$ and $\hat p_0$ the empirical zero fraction, where $\bar x_+$ is the positive sample mean. All-zero data give $p_0=1$ and leave $p$ unidentified. Holding either coefficient preserves attainment for compatible data. A free $p_0$ is unique, and a free $p$ is unique exactly when positives occur. Holding all coefficients leaves likelihood evaluation. Held $p_0=0$ excludes zeros, held $p_0=1$ excludes positives, and held $p=1$ permits positive counts only at one.
existence.reason: The likelihood factors into a Bernoulli zero-indicator likelihood and the positive geometric likelihood. For $k>0$ positive observations the latter is $p^k(1-p)^{\sum_{x_i>0}(x_i-1)}$, uniquely maximized at $p=k/\sum_{x_i>0}x_i$. This includes the attained endpoint $p=1$ when all positives are one. The Bernoulli factor is uniquely maximized at the empirical zero fraction. Without positives the likelihood is independent of $p$.

existence.statement: With both coefficients free, every nonempty sample of nonnegative integers has an MLE. The zero probability is the observed zero fraction. If there is a positive observation, the positive-count probability is unique, including $p=0$ when every positive count is one. With all-zero data, $p_0=1$ and $p$ is unidentified. existence.reason: The likelihood factors into the Bernoulli likelihood of the zero indicators and a logarithmic-series likelihood for the positive counts. The latter is a one-parameter exponential family with natural parameter $\log p$. Its mean increases strictly from one to infinity because its derivative in that parameter is its positive variance. Strict concavity therefore gives a unique root for a positive-count mean above one. At mean one the maximum is the attained member $p=0$. With no positive counts this factor is absent.

existence.statement: With all coefficients free, all-zero data attain a maximum at $p_0=1$ with unidentified base coefficients. Positive observations all equal to one attain a maximum at $p=1$ with size unidentified. For other samples, finite-size attainment depends on comparison with the infinite-size zero-modified Poisson boundary; general uniqueness is unknown. Holding any finite nonnegative size, or holding $0<p<1$, gives an attained maximum for compatible data. Holding only $p_0$ leaves the same positive-count existence problem. Further holds preserve these conclusions. Holding all coefficients leaves likelihood evaluation. Held zero-probability endpoints must match the observed zero indicators, and held $p=1$ permits positives only at one.
existence.reason: The zero-indicator factor is independent of the zero-truncated negative binomial likelihood of the positives. When positives occur, at fixed size it has a unique probability fit because its conditional mean is strictly monotone in the natural parameter; size zero is the continuous logarithmic-series member. At held $0<p<1$, its likelihood vanishes at infinite size and extends continuously to size zero, establishing attainment. With size and probability free, let $Q(r)$ be the maximized positive log likelihood at finite $r\ge0$ and let $Q_\infty$ be the fitted zero-truncated Poisson value. A finite maximum exists if some finite $r$ has $Q(r)\ge Q_\infty$; otherwise only the infinite-size boundary attains the supremum. The positive-count certificate establishes the required global ordering on each successful call; it stops on unresolved signs or extra extrema. At held interior probability the positive-count size fit is unique by strict concavity, as proved in the ztnbinom dossier.

These arguments do not establish unimodality or uniqueness of the free-size profile.

references: Dutang, C., Goulet, V. and Pigeon, M. (2008). actuar: An R Package for Actuarial Science. Journal of Statistical Software, 25(7), 1–37. doi:10.18637/jss.v025.i07.

existence.statement: For every nonempty sample of positive integers, the free-rate MLE exists and is unique. It is $\hat\lambda=0$ when all observations equal one. Otherwise it is the unique positive solution of $\lambda/(1-e^{-\lambda})=\bar x$. Holding the rate leaves only likelihood evaluation. A held zero rate requires every observation to equal one.
existence.reason: In the natural parameter $\eta=\log\lambda$, the second derivative of the log likelihood is minus the sample size times the conditional variance, which is strictly negative. The conditional mean increases continuously from one to infinity as the rate increases from zero to infinity. Thus every sample mean above one gives exactly one score root. At mean one the attained zero-rate member maximizes the likelihood.

reference.method: damped Newton at 50 digits on the README log density, from the fitted values
